The fact that judicial opinions have left much of the interpretation of 
Article n unsettled does not imply a history of continuous harmonious 
adjustment between the two elected branches. Ambiguity or vagueness 
concernmg the powers of the executive almost always suggests the 
possibility of legislative power. The brevity of Article 11 thus leads not to a 
power vacuum but to a power struggle. The battle began in the first 
Congress (see I An n a l s OF CONGRESS 473-608 (1789)) concerning the 
removal power (see Burkoff, supra, at 1379-83), and has been raging ever 
since. This is a pohtical war with many truces but no possibility of a 
comprehensive, stable peace treaty. Neither the president nor the Congress 
IS a political lightweight; the pohtical stakes are often high; and each has 
regular opportunities to encroach on domains claimed by the other.
Consider, for example, the techniques avahable to the modern 
president to shape administrative pohcy. First, the president possesses 
powers to appoint, and to remove, agency officials. These powers are 
amplified by the authority to issue executive orders, directives, or simple 
statements of pohcy, sometimes recently in the form of mere social media 
posts. The president can also explore possibihties for agency organization 
and reorganization, impose informal or exphcit requirements for 
interagency coordination, pubhcly support or withhold support for the 
actions of an administrative agency, and demand central clearance of 
budget requests and legislative proposals. Lying behind these various 
carrots and sticks are others, ranging from the Attorney General’s control 
over agency htigation to the president’s unique access to the media
Congress, however, has powers to check and balance the president. 
Appointments can be blocked and removals of at least some officers 
conditioned by statute on “cause.” Congress may delegate authority to 
appoint and remove to officials other than the president. Agencies can be 
set up as independent,” either within or outside the Executive branch- 
agency budgets can be cut, expanded, or restricted from being used for a 
particifiar purpose; statutory administrative powers can be altered 
, 
withheld. Presidential ambitions for new legislation may be
held hostage to congressional desires for administrative changes of 
direction. Congressional oversight hearings may be structured to 
embarrass the president politically. Even impeachment, while rare is not 
unknown.
To be sure, not all the things the president and the Congress might do 
as they contend for political control of administration are necessarily 
consistent with the Constitution. Indeed, because virtually every technique 
available to one contestant has implications for the reserved powers of the 
o er, each thrust and parry necessarily raises an issue of separation of 
powers. Moreover, certain forms of uiterbranch competition for control of
